scope: 35 local Rust arithmetic calendar conversion, era, field limit and typed calendar arithmetic dependencies. Implementation and requirement statuses unchanged.
source_comparison: Frozen Temporal proposal via durable checklist rows. ECMA-262 remains requested authority.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §3.3.3 step 3: expose the selected arithmetic calendar name.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Returns the static canonical name of each of the 13 arithmetic enum variants. CalendarProvider uses it as its ID transport; the public slot read and string conversion are separately owned.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.10 step 4: select the arithmetic calendar for a prepared name.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Exact match selects a supported arithmetic enum, including finite aliases for ethioaa and islamic-civil. Unknown names return None. Case handling, table calendar discovery and complete Unicode calendar canonicalization belong to callers.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §3.3.11 step 3: compute the year boundary used by day-of-year.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Checks supported year then computes an exact year start using civil offsets, arithmetic cycles or the Hebrew postponement helper. Native day-of-year and days-in-year callers use one or two such starts. Provider accuracy and finite chronology proofs remain distinct.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §3.3.17 step 3: read the arithmetic calendar month count.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Checks supported year and returns 13 for the fixed thirteen-month calendars and Hebrew leap years; otherwise 12. Field transport and public getter behavior remain separate.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §3.3.15 step 3: calculate month length for the validated calendar month.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Validates ordinal and calendar year. Gregorian-family branch uses standard month lengths and the adjusted civil leap year. Other branches reuse their year length or defining month rules; their implementation-defined semantics are separate.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §3.3.8 step 3: map the ordinal to its month code.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Checks ordinal, then emits the leap instance M05L for Hebrew leap ordinal six and adjusts later ordinary codes. Other calendars preserve their ordinal as an ordinary code.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.31 step 2.a: resolve the month code to an ordinal.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Validates code range/calendar support. Hebrew M05L resolves to ordinal six and rejects an absent leap month in reject mode. Ordinary codes shift after the inserted month in a leap year. Caller checks explicit month agreement.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.12 steps 2–3: convert fields and check the ordinary date range.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Delegates typed fields and overflow to raw epoch-day conversion then validates the ordinary result day. Object allocation and exception conversion remain outside.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.31 step 2.a: resolve the month code before date conversion.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Typed entrypoint resolves code and reuses checked ordinary conversion with the same overflow. Field-record preparation and mismatch policy belong to higher-level callers.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.22 steps 1.b, 2: regulate fields and accumulate the epoch day.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Select ordinal month under overflow before computing its day bound. Sum year start, lengths of prior months and one-based day offset. This supplies carried ISO-day representation without public coercion or object-range validation.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.26 steps 1.b, 2: project a checked epoch day.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Checks the ordinary day range and delegates exact calendar field projection. Additional public calendar fields are assembled by callers.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.26 steps 1.b, 2: extract civil or arithmetic calendar fields.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Checks the extended domain and uses ISO inverse fields directly for Gregorian-based calendars, applying year-label offsets where needed. Other branches correct their estimate against year starts then subtract month lengths. Proofs bound the accepted chronology and termination.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.7 step 2.a: get the serial month prefix for calendar arithmetic.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Checks supported year and returns the fixed-count product or Hebrew 235-month/19-year prefix. Shared add/difference use these private coordinates; the epoch order proof is separate.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.7 step 2.a: recover calendar year and month from a serial.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Checks serial magnitude, estimates year by fixed count or Hebrew cycle, and adjusts to the enclosing prefix. Converts the residual to one-based ordinal. Finite bounds and exact inverse are in the chronology proof.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.7 steps 1, 2.a: delegate calendar addition on raw days.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Routes typed date duration, epoch and overflow into shared NumericCalendar arithmetic. Raw path leaves final object range checks to caller.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.7 steps 2.a, 3: add calendar fields and check the result day.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Checks ordinary input day, performs the shared typed addition and rejects an out-of-range result day. Shared owner handles balancing/constraining.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.26 steps 1.b, 2: project a private extended reference day.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Forwards to raw inverse with its wider guard rather than ordinary day range. Short-date callers retain their own YearMonth/MonthDay object limits.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.13 step 3: convert fields in the wider reference-day range.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Applies raw calendar conversion and the wider coordinate guard. Caller chooses representative fields and checks object-specific limits.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §9.5.8 step 12: add a duration to an extended reference date.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Delegates to shared raw addition and checks the wider result coordinate. YearMonth logic owns construction of the starting reference day and the final object.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.9 steps 3–4: check input days and route date difference.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Validates both ordinary day endpoints, forwards largest unit to raw difference. Does not resolve known ISO comparison issues or prove provider-wide policy.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.9 steps 3–4: delegate date difference on typed endpoints.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Routes ISO and non-ISO day difference to shared NumericCalendar arithmetic. Result decomposition and prefix behavior are callee-owned and have separate audits.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §3.3.4 and §3.3.5 step 3: check the day before projecting era fields.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Validates an ordinary epoch day, then reuses extended era projection. JS receiver checking and primitive result creation remain caller-owned.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §9.3.4 and §9.3.5 step 3: project era fields on an extended day.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Converts the extended date and forwards it alongside the epoch to era selection. The original epoch enables precise Japanese transition-day comparison.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.26 steps 1.b, 2: supply era name and year for the projected date.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Uses selected calendar and date to choose era fields. ISO has no era. Japanese compares day boundaries, while named negative-era calendars map nonpositive years to one minus the year. Caller owns the public record representation.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.31 step 2.a: resolve an era year to the calendar year.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Maps supported typed era names to calendar years, applying negative-era, Ethiopic or Japanese offsets and rejecting unknown eras. Checks result bounds before narrowing. Frontend name normalization and explicit year agreement stay separate.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §3.5.7 steps 1.a, 1.c, 2.b: clamp or reject a bounded field.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Typed constrain clamps to supplied bounds; reject errors when out of bounds. Raw conversion chooses month bound first and day bound from the resulting month.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §3.5.12 step 2: check the inclusive ordinary epoch-day range.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Returns the day within inclusive −100000001 through 100000000, otherwise a typed range failure. This encodes the ordinary noon-based PlainDate limit, distinct from Instant and extended caller ranges.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §9.5.8 step 12: guard private reference-day arithmetic.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Checks implementation-internal ±110000000 result coordinates. This wider guard supplies short-date and rounding helpers without substituting for public object limits.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.17 step 4: detect a Gregorian leap year.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Uses exact Euclidean divisibility by four with century exclusion and four-hundred-year inclusion. Works for negative as well as positive civil years.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.26 step 2: determine whether a Hebrew year adds a month.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Tests the 19-year cycle by exact Euclidean remainder. Supplies the Hebrew month count, month-code conversion and date projection branch.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.26 step 2: compute the Hebrew year-start postponement input.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Builds the Hebrew month serial and base molad day by exact Euclidean integer arithmetic, then applies the local weekday correction consumed by hebrew_start.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §12.3.26 step 2: compute the Hebrew year boundary.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Applies the epoch shift and adjacent-year postponement conditions. Finite Hebrew proof checks year lengths and alignment across the supported domain.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §13.1 steps 3–4: convert prepared civil fields to a Unix epoch day.
reviewed_rows.evidence: March-based Gregorian 400-year eras and exact month prefixes recover the Unix day count for normalized civil fields. Caller owns month normalization and validation.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §11.1.10 step 2: precompute year blocks for inverse ISO projection.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Each 128-day checkpoint stores bounded within-era year, day ordinal and leap flag. The existing comparison proof derives the civil inverse from these packed coordinates.

reviewed_rows.annotation: // Proposal comparison §11.1.10 step 2: recover ISO date fields from an exact epoch day.
reviewed_rows.evidence: Euclidean division selects 400-year era and bounded block. At most one year boundary occurs in a 128-day block. Integer month extraction reverses the March-origin shift without float conversion.
